title: Multifunctionality in Janus CrMCN4 (M = Si/Ge) Monolayers: Valleytronic Physics, Piezoelectric Response, and Photocatalytic Potential
authors: Jubair Hossan Abir, M. R. U. S. Shapon, S. S. B. Pallab, Tanvir Khan, Raihana Shams Islam, Saleh Hasan Naqib
abstract: Two dimensional Janus semiconductors integrating spin-valley coupling, piezoelectricity, and tunable optical responses offer a platform for multifunctional nanodevices. Here, first-principles calculations reveal complementary composition and strain effects in CrSiCN4 and CrGeCN4 monolayers. Both are found to be nonmagnetic direct-gap semiconductors, with gaps of 1.23 and 1.09 eV using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional including spin-orbit coupling, respectively. HSE06 hybrid-functional calculations retain the direct-gap character, yielding gaps of 1.46 eV for CrSiCN4 and 1.19 eV for CrGeCN4. Opposite out-of-plane spin character and Berry curvature emerge at K and K'. Biaxial strain reduces the respective gaps from 1.59 to 0.86 eV and 1.44 to 0.63 eV, drives direct-to-indirect transitions, and redshifts absorption while preserving valley spin contrast. CrGeCN4 exhibits larger in-plane piezoelectric response, whereas CrSiCN4 exhibits larger out-of-plane magnitude. Band-edge alignment satisfies the oxygen evolution reaction requirement but provides insufficient driving force for the hydrogen evolution reaction, motivating further strain-induced band-edge modulation toward overall water splitting. These results establish composition and strain as complementary controls for tailoring Cr-based Janus monolayers for valleytronic, optoelectronic, electromechanical, and photocatalytic applications.
summary: This theoretical study explores the multifunctional potential of Janus $	ext{CrMCN}_4$ monolayers by calculating how strain and composition tune their electronic, piezoelectric, and optical properties. The findings demonstrate that these materials can be engineered to exhibit desirable characteristics for valleytronic, energy harvesting, and electromechanical applications.
main_problem: The study investigates the potential for multifunctional nanodevices using Janus $	ext{CrMCN}_4$ ($	ext{M} = 	ext{Si/Ge}$) monolayers, focusing on the interplay between valleytronics, piezoelectricity, and photocatalysis.
main_result: The research establishes that composition ($	ext{Si}$ vs $	ext{Ge}$) and external strain are complementary methods to tailor these monolayers for diverse applications, controlling band gaps, piezoelectric response, and spin-valley characteristics.
method: The work relies heavily on first-principles Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations, employing advanced functionals like HSE06 and incorporating spin-orbit coupling (SOC) to model electronic, structural, and optical properties.
model_or_system: The physical system is the two-dimensional Janus semiconductor $	ext{CrMCN}_4$ monolayer, which exhibits an asymmetric septuple-layer architecture. The calculations model the effect of biaxial strain ($\pm 4\%$) on the electronic and structural properties.
key_observables: Band gaps (PBE+SOC and HSE06), piezoelectric coefficients ($d_{ij}$), Berry curvature, spin-valley polarization, and optical absorption spectra.
important_parameters: Biaxial strain ($\epsilon$), SOC strength, and the choice of metal ($	ext{Si}$ or $	ext{Ge}$) in the lattice structure.
main_assumptions: The calculations assume the validity of DFT methods and the ability to model complex phenomena like spin-valley coupling and piezoelectricity using first principles.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate strain-dependent optical absorption spectra, strain effects on electronic and spin-dependent properties (band gaps, spin splitting), and comparisons between different theoretical calculations.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the electronic structure, detailing the impact of composition ($	ext{Si}$ vs $	ext{Ge}$) and strain on the band gap, spin character, and polarization. It then separately addresses the piezoelectric response and the photocatalytic potential for water splitting.
why_interesting: The detailed theoretical prediction of multiple coupled quantum phenomena (valley, spin, electric polarization) in a single 2D material platform is highly relevant for designing next-generation quantum-functional materials.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Optimized geometrical structures of monolayer CrMCN4 (M = Si and Ge). The side view (left) and top view (right) depict the atomic configuration of the monolayers, showing the arrangement of Cr, C, N, and Si/Ge atoms. The corresponding unit cell and crystallographic directions are also indicated.

Figure 2. Electronic properties of monolayer CrSiCN4 and CrGeCN4 calculated using the HSE06 functional without spin-orbit coupling (SOC). (a, b) Electronic band structures of CrSiCN4 and CrGeCN4, respectively. The corresponding projected density of states (PDOS) is shown alongside the band structures. The band-decomposed charge densities of the valence band maximum (VBM) and conduction band minimum (CBM), together with the planar-averaged electrostatic potential distribution along the out-of-plane (Z) direction, are also presented.

Figure 3. SOC-induced spin splitting and valley-dependent electronic structures of monolayer (a) CrSiCN4 and (b) CrGeCN4 obtained using PBE+SOC calculations. The band gaps are marked by blue arrows, while the enlarged K/K′ valley regions show the conduction band (Δc) and valence band (Δv) spin splittings. Red and blue arrows indicate valley-selective optical transitions coupled with right and left-handed circularly polarized light, respectively. The color map represents the spin expectation value along the z direction (⟨Sz⟩) of the spinor states.
Figure 4. Orbital-projected band structures of monolayer (a)CrSiCN4 and (b)CrGeCN4, illustrating the orbital contributions of Cr-d, Si/Ge-p, C-p, and N-p states near the band edges.

Figure 5. Schematic illustration of a strain-tunable spin-valley / valley Hall device based on Janus CrMCN4 (M =Si, Ge). The monolayer channel is integrated on a flexible substrate between source and drain electrodes with back gate. Biaxial tensile strain modulates the electronic structure and enhances transverse Hall-voltage response. Charge accumulation at opposite channel edges produce a measurable Hall voltage VH.
